---
title: "Non-normal likelihood approximations"
subtitle: "When the per-estimate normal assumption breaks"
---

## Two normal assumptions, only one of them safe

The [empirical null](null-distribution.qmd) makes two separate normality
assumptions, and they deserve different levels of trust.

The first is that the **systematic error across hypotheses** is normal,
$\epsilon \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$. This is a modelling choice about a population
of biases, and it is reasonable in the way most random-effects assumptions are.

The second is that **each individual estimate's likelihood** is normal — that
$\hat\beta_i$ with standard error $\hat\sigma_i$ captures everything the data
say about hypothesis $i$. This is an asymptotic approximation, and it fails
exactly where safety surveillance lives: rare outcomes, few events, early looks
in a sequential analysis. With three events the true likelihood for a log rate
ratio is markedly skewed, and summarising it by a point and a symmetric standard
error throws away the shape.

`fitNullNonNormalLl` and `calibrateLlr` keep the first assumption and drop the
second.

## The generalised likelihood

If hypothesis $i$ contributes an arbitrary likelihood function $L_i(x)$ over the
true log relative risk $x$, rather than a normal one, the null's likelihood
becomes a convolution:

::: {.keyresult}
$$
\ell(\mu, \sigma) \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^{n}
\log \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \phi(x;\, \mu,\, \sigma)\; L_i(x)\ dx .
$$
:::

Each term integrates that control's likelihood against the null density: the
probability of the data for control $i$, averaged over the systematic errors the
null says are possible. Substituting a normal $L_i$ recovers the closed form
$\phi(\hat\beta_i; \mu, \sqrt{\sigma^2 + \hat\sigma_i^2})$ from before, so this
is a strict generalisation.

There is no closed form for general $L_i$, so the integral is evaluated
numerically over $\mu \pm 10\sigma$ for every control at every optimiser step.
That makes `fitNullNonNormalLl` substantially slower than `fitNull` — seconds
rather than milliseconds.

## The four shapes

The function detects which of four representations you passed from the columns
present, and prints what it detected.

### Normal

Columns `logRr`, `seLogRr`. Detected first, and short-circuits straight to
`fitNull` — no integration.

$$
\log L(x) = \log \phi(x;\, \hat\beta,\, \hat\sigma)
$$

### Custom parametric

Columns `mu`, `sigma`, `gamma`. A skewed three-parameter form used by some OHDSI
analytics packages to summarise a likelihood profile compactly:

$$
\log L(x) \;=\; e^{\gamma (x - \mu)} \cdot \frac{-(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}
$$

$\gamma = 0$ gives back a normal log-likelihood; $\gamma \ne 0$ tilts it.

### Skew normal

Columns `mu`, `sigma`, `alpha`.

$$
\log L(x) \;=\; \log 2 \;+\; \log\phi\!\left(x; \mu, \sigma\right)
\;+\; \log\Phi\!\left(\alpha (x - \mu);\, 0,\, \sigma\right)
$$

$\alpha$ is the skewness; $\alpha = 0$ is exactly normal.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## A numerical detail that matters

The last term is computed with a log-scale normal CDF rather than
`log(pnorm(...))`. Over a $\pm 10\sigma$ integration range the argument routinely
drops below $-38$, where the probability underflows to zero and its logarithm to
$-\infty$, silently poisoning the integral. Computing the log directly keeps it
finite.
:::

### Grid

A likelihood **profile**: the log-likelihood evaluated on a grid of points, with
no parametric form imposed at all. This is the most faithful representation and
the one to prefer when the analytics package can emit it.

Two layouts are accepted. A data frame with columns `point` and `value` is one
profile. A data frame whose *column names* are the grid points and whose rows
are profiles handles many controls at once — the layout OHDSI likelihood-profile
exports use.

Between grid points the log-likelihood is linearly interpolated. Outside the
grid it is linearly extrapolated with the slope clamped so the profile can only
stay flat or decrease — an unbounded likelihood outside the profiled region
would otherwise let the optimiser run away.

## Worked example

Build grid profiles from simulated controls and confirm the fit recovers the
same answer the asymptotic route gives:

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import empiricalcalibration as ec
from empiricalcalibration._rmath import dnorm

ec.set_seed(123)
data = ec.simulateControls(n=50, mean=0.2, sd=0.2, trueLogRr=0, seLogRr=0.1)

asymptotic = ec.fitNull(data.logRr, data.seLogRr)

point = np.linspace(np.log(0.1), np.log(10), 1000)
profiles = [
    pd.DataFrame({"point": point,
                  "value": dnorm(point, data.logRr.iloc[i], data.seLogRr.iloc[i])})
    for i in range(len(data))
]
from_grid = ec.fitNullNonNormalLl(profiles)
```

```{python}
print(f"asymptotic:  mean {asymptotic[0]:.4f}  sd {asymptotic[1]:.4f}")
print(f"from grids:  mean {from_grid[0]:.4f}  sd {from_grid[1]:.4f}")
```

The profiles here were *built* from normal likelihoods, so agreement is the
correct outcome and a check that the grid machinery is faithful. The reason to
use the grid path in practice is the case where the profiles are **not** normal,
and there the two routes will legitimately disagree — the grid answer being the
better one.

## Where it flows through

The same four representations are accepted by `calibrateLlr`, so a sequential
surveillance analysis can carry non-normal likelihoods end to end: fit the null
from profiles, then calibrate the LLR from profiles. See
[MaxSPRT](maxsprt.qmd).

`calibrateP`, by contrast, takes a point estimate and standard error — the
calibrated p-value has a closed form only under normality. To calibrate a
non-normal estimate, work with the LLR instead.

## API

| Function | Accepts |
|---|---|
| [`fitNullNonNormalLl(likelihoodApproximations)`](../reference/index.qmd#fitnullnonnormalll) | frame of normal / custom / skew-normal parameters, wide grid frame, or list of profiles |
| [`calibrateLlr(null, likelihoodApproximation)`](../reference/index.qmd#calibratellr) | the same four forms |

Rows with missing parameters are dropped with a warning. A frame whose column
names are neither recognised parameter names nor parseable as numbers raises
`ValueError`.
